content: Between 1990 and 2001, a total of 534 cases of tetanus were reported in the United States. Among these, 301 cases (56%) occurred in adults aged 19–64 years, and 201 cases (38%) occurred in adults aged 65 years or older (CDC, unpublished data, 2005). The prevalence of protective antibody levels against tetanus (≥0.15 IU/mL) was greater than 80% among adults aged 20–39 years but declined with increasing age. Among individuals aged over 70 years, 45% of men and 21% of women had protective antibody levels (98). The low prevalence of immunity and the high proportion of tetanus cases among older adults may be attributed to the significant number of older individuals, particularly women, who never received a primary vaccination series (96, 97). Neonatal tetanus typically results from Clostridium tetani infection of the umbilical stump. Susceptible infants are born to mothers with insufficient maternal tetanus antitoxin levels to provide passive immunity (95). Neonatal tetanus is rare in the United States, with only three cases reported (CDC, unpublished data, 2005). Two of these infants were born to mothers who had either not received any doses or had received only one dose of a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (99, 100). The vaccination history of the third mother was unknown (CDC, unpublished data, 2005). Strong evidence supports the recommendation for tetanus toxoid vaccination during pregnancy for previously unvaccinated women (33, 95, 103–105). In 1999, the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and the United Nations Population Fund adopted a global goal to eliminate maternal and neonatal tetanus (104). Respiratory diphtheria is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae or other corynebacteria (e.g., C. ulcerans) that produce diphtheria toxin. The disease is preventable through vaccination with diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines. Respiratory diphtheria is characterized by the presence of a grayish, adherent membrane in the pharynx, palate, or nasal mucosa, which can obstruct the airway. Systemic complications mediated by the diphtheria toxin, such as cardiac and neurologic effects, can also occur (105, 106). Reports of respiratory diphtheria are rare in the United States (107, 108). Between 1998 and 2004, seven cases of respiratory diphtheria were reported to the CDC (9, 10). The last culture-confirmed case of respiratory diphtheria caused by C. diphtheriae in an adult aged over 19 years was reported in 2000 (108). A case of respiratory diphtheria caused by C. ulcerans in an adult was reported in 2005 (CDC, unpublished data, 2005). The prevalence of protective antibody levels against diphtheria (≥0.1 IU/mL) decreases with age, from 91% in children aged 6–11 years to approximately 30% in individuals aged 60–69 years (98). Adherence to the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)-recommended schedule of decennial tetanus-diphtheria (Td) boosters in adults is critical to prevent sporadic cases of respiratory diphtheria and to maintain population immunity (33). Cases of diphtheria in the United States are typically associated with imported cases or rare endemic toxin-producing strains of corynebacteria other than C. diphtheriae (106). The clinical management of diphtheria, including the use of diphtheria antitoxin, and the public health response are reviewed elsewhere (33, 106, 109). In the United States, one Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis) vaccine product is licensed for use in adults and adolescents. Adacel® (Sanofi Pasteur, Toronto, Ontario, Canada) was licensed on June 10, 2005, for use in individuals aged 11–64 years as a single-dose booster vaccination against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (11). Another Tdap product, Boostrix® (GlaxoSmithKline, Rixensart, Belgium), is licensed for use in adolescents but not for individuals aged over 19 years (20). Adacel® contains the same tetanus toxoid, diphtheria toxoid, and five pertussis antigens as Daptacel® (pediatric DTaP), but it is formulated with reduced quantities of diphtheria toxoid and detoxified pertussis toxin (PT). Each antigen is adsorbed onto aluminum phosphate and includes 5 µg detoxified PT, 5 µg filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA), 3 µg pertactin (PRN), and 5 µg fimbriae types 2 and 3 (FIM) in a 0.5-mL dose. Adacel® does not contain thimerosal and is available in single-dose vials that are latex-free (11). In a non-inferiority trial, immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety endpoints were demonstrated when a new product was at least as effective as a comparator based on a predefined and narrow margin for clinically acceptable differences between study groups (110). Adolescents aged 11–17 years were also studied, and these results are reported elsewhere (12, 111, 112).
